questions.q: Identify the grammatical term for the sentence structure in Manjula's line: "My speech will last exactly ten minutes. I have timed it... No, I won't read. 'Look ahead and speak!' Good... But that may take a little longer."
questions.a: The structure exemplifies **ellipsis** (omission of understood words) and **fragmented syntax** — "No, I won't read" omits the subject-verb "I will" after "No"; "Good..." stands alone as a discourse marker. A wrong answer like "simple sentences" misses the conversational, real-time processing quality that characterizes her unscripted moments versus her prepared speech. This reveals whether the student distinguishes between *sentence types* (declarative/interrogative) and *syntactic completeness* in dramatic dialogue.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Karnad includes Kannada terms like *prayashchitta*, *arthapoorna*, and *Namaskara* without translation in an English-language play. What grammatical function do they serve in the utterance?
questions.a: These are **code-switched lexical insertions** functioning as **cultural deictics** — they index Manjula's Kannada identity and resist full assimilation into English. Grammatically, they operate as **unassimilated loanwords** retaining their morphological integrity (no English pluralization, no articles) and pragmatic force (*prayashchitta* carries ritual weight "absolution" cannot). A wrong answer like "they add local colour" treats them as decorative rather than functional; it misses how code-switching here performs the play's central argument: that English cannot fully capture the "Kannada reality" Manjula inhabits.

questions.q: Apply the concept of **register shift** to analyze the difference between the Announcer's opening ("Many of you will know her as a renowned Kannada short-story writer...") and Manjula's aside to the Image ("Aw, shut up!"). Provide one grammatical feature that distinguishes each register.
questions.a: The Announcer uses **formal public register**: passive voice ("will be broadcast"), complex pre-modification ("the Literary Phenomenon of the Decade"), and third-person reference. Manjula's aside uses **intimate informal register**: imperative verb ("shut up"), contraction-ready syntax, and zero politeness markers. A student who only notes "one is formal, one is informal" without citing grammatical evidence (passive vs. imperative, nominalization vs. verb-first) has not *applied* register analysis — they've only labeled it.

questions.q: Analyze how the stage direction "(Laughs.)" functions grammatically and pragmatically when it appears mid-utterance versus at utterance-end. Compare: "But when you think of Indian television studios, you always imagine them cluttered. (Laughs.)" vs. "I have timed it... No, I won't read. (Laughs.)"
questions.a: Mid-utterance "(Laughs.)" acts as a **parenthetical discourse marker** signaling self-awareness/irony *during* the speech act — it frames the preceding clause as performative. Utterance-final "(Laughs.)" functions as a **terminal prosodic cue** closing the turn with affiliative intent. Grammatically, the first interrupts the syntactic flow (anacoluthon); the second follows a complete illocutionary act. A wrong answer treats both as identical "stage directions" — missing how Karnad uses laughter's *position* to distinguish Manjula's calculated charm (mid-speech) from genuine release (post-speech).

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The Image's language is grammatically simpler than Manjula's, proving it is a lesser, artificial version of her." Use two specific grammatical comparisons from the text to defend or refute.
questions.a: The claim is **false**. The Image uses *more* interrogatives ("Where are you going?", "What are you screaming for?"), *more* elliptical imperatives ("Aw, screw the film..."), and *sharper* syntactic parallelism ("Me? You.") — features of **analytical, probing discourse**, not simplicity. Manjula's language includes more hedging ("I think," "perhaps," "sort of"), false starts, and self-correction — markers of *cognitive load* and *performance anxiety*. The Image's grammatical precision reflects its role as unflinching truth-teller. A student accepting the claim confuses *formal complexity* with *psychological depth*.

questions.q: Create a 4-line dialogue exchange between Manjula and the Image that uses **syntactic mirroring** (repeating the other's structure with a key lexical substitution) to reveal a new layer of their conflict. Annotate the grammatical pattern you employed.
questions.a:
**Example:**
MANJULA: I wrote the novel *for* her.
IMAGE: You wrote the novel *from* her.
MANJULA: I dedicated it *to* her.
IMAGE: You built a career *on* her.

**Pattern:** Syntactic mirroring via **preposition substitution** in identical SVO+PP frames. Each line replicates the subject-verb-object-prepositional phrase structure, swapping only the preposition (*for/from/to/on*) to shift semantic agency from love → extraction → tribute → exploitation. A poor answer would merely repeat words without structural control, missing how grammatical parallelism creates the *inescapable logic* of the Image's critique.
